title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Admission, Transfer & Discharge
html:
Admission, transfer, and discharge are high-risk transitions because responsibility, information, medications, equipment, and follow-up plans must move safely with the client. The RN verifies the person and immediate safety, establishes a reliable baseline, communicates changes, anticipates barriers, and confirms that the next care setting can carry out the plan.

Learning goals

  • Complete admission safety priorities before routine tasks.
  • Establish an accurate physical, functional, psychosocial, and medication baseline.
  • Prepare and communicate a safe transfer of responsibility.
  • Begin discharge planning early and identify barriers to the plan.
  • Use plain language and teach-back to evaluate discharge understanding.

Admission: stabilize, identify, and establish a baseline

Use the required identifiers, confirm allergies and immediate precautions, and begin with a primary survey of airway, breathing, circulation, and level of consciousness. Address instability before completing routine forms. Reconcile available orders and medications, assess pain and fall risk, examine skin and devices, establish vital-sign and functional baselines, and ask about communication, sensory, cultural, spiritual, cognitive, and access needs.

Invite the client and support person, with permission, to describe goals, concerns, usual routines, and what will make the transition safe. Record belongings and valuables according to policy. Orient the client to the environment, call system, toileting plan, team, and how to ask for help. Admission assessment is comprehensive but remains prioritized: urgent cues come before completeness.

Discharge planning begins at admission
Ask early about the anticipated destination, caregiver availability, mobility and equipment needs, transportation, medication access, health literacy, language services, home environment, and follow-up barriers. Waiting until departure day can make an otherwise correct plan unsafe or impossible.

Transfer: move responsibility with the client

Before an internal or external transfer, reassess stability and confirm that the receiving setting is prepared for the client. Verify the destination, transport level, required equipment, oxygen or monitoring needs, lines and drains, medications due, infection precautions, and records or specimens that must accompany the client. Follow policy for valuables and personal items.

Give a structured handoff that includes identifiers, current condition and trends, relevant history, allergies, code status when applicable, recent changes, medications and treatments, devices, safety risks, pending tests, time-sensitive tasks, and what requires reassessment. Allow questions and use read-back or check-back when required. Document the transfer, accepting clinician or location, client condition, and communication completed.

Discharge: build a plan the client can use

Confirm the discharge order and readiness process, reconcile the medication list, and explain which medicines continue, change, or stop according to the final plan. Review the condition and self-care instructions, activity and diet directions, equipment or wound care, pending results, follow-up appointments, contact information, and specific warning signs—including when to call the clinic, seek urgent help, or use emergency services.

Use plain language, a qualified interpreter when needed, and written or accessible materials suited to the client. Include the chosen caregiver with permission. Assess whether prescriptions, transportation, equipment, home services, food, housing, cognition, dexterity, vision, cost, or caregiving capacity create a barrier. Escalate unresolved barriers rather than documenting that teaching was completed and sending the client into an unsafe situation.

Teach-back evaluates the explanation

Teach-back is not a quiz of the client. Ask the client to explain the plan in their own words or demonstrate a skill so the team can judge whether the explanation was clear. For example: “To make sure I explained it clearly, please show me how you will take this medicine at home.” If understanding is incomplete, clarify in a different way and reassess. A nod, signature, or “yes” alone does not demonstrate readiness.

Evaluate the transition

Before responsibility changes, verify the client's current stability, the accuracy and completeness of information, receipt of required medications and equipment, understanding of warning signs and follow-up, and the receiving person's opportunity to ask questions. Document unresolved issues and who owns the next action. A safe transition closes the loop; it does not end when transportation arrives.

Clinical example

A client scheduled for discharge correctly repeats the new medication schedule but reveals during teach-back that the pharmacy is closed and no ride is available until the next day. The RN recognizes an access barrier, pauses the departure process as appropriate, and collaborates with the discharge team on a workable plan. Repeating the instructions would not solve the actual risk.
